meta:
Consumer Discretionary · Movies & Entertainment · ~$173B mkt cap
Fiscal years 2021–2025 · annual & long-term incentive plans
thesis: A profitability-disciplined plan whose stock-based half kept paying zero. The annual bonus is stable every year — 35% segment operating income, 17.5% revenue, 17.5% after-tax free cash flow, 30% other factors — and has paid 97–191% as parks and the streaming pivot recovered. The long-term plan is 50% relative TSR (vs. the S&P 500) + 50% return on invested capital, but relative TSR paid 0% in all three completed cycles, so the equity earned out only on ROIC (49–73%).
orientation_caption: Horizontal: profitability (left) to growth (right). Vertical: shareholder return (top) to other (bottom). Net weight tilt on each axis, AIP and LTIP blended equally. Relative TSR is a weighted LTIP metric here (not a modifier), so it places the dot rather than appearing as an arrow.
orientation_note: DIS sits firmly in Capital Discipline (profitability + shareholder return), heavily profitability-led: segment operating income and free cash flow dominate the AIP, and ROIC is half the LTIP. FY21–24 cluster at one point; FY25 shifts further left as the new LTIP grant added Adjusted EPS Growth (50%) and cut the relative-TSR weight from 50% to 25% — more profitability emphasis, less market-relative. Growth weight is low because revenue is only 17.5% of the AIP and absent from the LTIP.
goalpost_caption: Bar spans threshold → maximum in reported dollars; notch is target; dot is actual. The three AIP financial metrics carry clean disclosed bands; segment operating income and free cash flow crossed from negative to positive over the period (the FY21 COVID trough), so the zero line is shown. Green ≥ max, gold in-band, red below threshold.

matrix_rows.group: Annual incentive (AIP) — stable four-factor structure every year
matrix_rows.name: Adjusted segment operating income

matrix_rows.group: Long-term incentive (LTIP) — 3-yr cycle, 50% rel. TSR + 50% ROIC (FY25 adds EPS growth)
matrix_rows.name: Relative TSR (S&P 500)

matrix_note: Two CEOs span the window (Chapek FY21–22, Iger FY23–25), so the AIP series is not fully continuous. The AIP structure itself held constant: 35% segment operating income, 17.5% revenue, 17.5% free cash flow, 30% other factors. LTIP rows are shown in the grant-start year column: relative TSR paid 0% in all three completed cycles (Disney underperformed the S&P 500 through the streaming-investment years), so the equity earned out on ROIC alone, completing at 66.9%, 73.4% and 48.9% of target. The FY25 grant restructured to 25% rel. TSR + 25% ROIC + 50% adjusted EPS growth and switched the TSR benchmark to a media-and-entertainment index.
pay_structure_caption: Long-term award composition by grant year as % of target award. DIS dropped RSUs after FY22, moving to a PSU + options mix.
pay_legend: PSUs (TSR / ROIC / EPS)RSUsOptions
pay_structure_note: FY21–22 grants split 50% PSU / 25% RSU / 25% options; from FY23 RSUs were dropped for a 60% PSU / 40% options mix. PSUs vest on relative TSR and ROIC (plus adjusted EPS growth from the FY25 grant). Regular CEO target award value rose to $30–35M for Iger. Excludes small ROIC-only special PSU grants and the additive annual cash bonus.

realization.note: Targets differ by CEO: Chapek carried a $2.5M base / 300% target; Iger a $1.0M base / 500% target. Opportunity ceiling is 200% of target. The FY23 realized figure ($2.14M) is well below the others despite a 113% multiplier — Iger's first bonus was prorated for his partial (return) year — so it is not comparable to the full-year FY24/FY25 payouts. Bar fills shown as closeness-to-cap.

classification_rule: Classification rule. Metrics are bucketed by underlying measure, not verb. Segment operating income, free cash flow, ROIC and adjusted EPS growth → profitability. Revenue → growth. Relative TSR vs. the S&P 500 → shareholder return (a weighted LTIP metric here, so it places the dot). The AIP “Other Performance Factors” (D&I/talent, synergy, storytelling & creativity) → other. AIP and LTIP weighted equally.
provenance_html: CEO succession (March 18, 2026). After the FY25 window, Robert Iger stepped down as CEO and became a senior adviser; Josh D'Amaro (former Chairman of Disney Experiences) was appointed CEO and to the Board (Item 5.02). At the same March 18 annual meeting, the say-on-pay vote drew a striking ~14% against (1.09B for vs. 181.8M against) — the loudest pay dissent among large consumer names this cycle, consistent with the long-term plan's repeated zero TSR payouts. No special or off-cadence mega-grant was found in the research record (only minor ROIC-only PSU true-ups).
footer: Sources: Verity / InsiderScore incentive-plan data (annual & long-term), proxy statements, research, and SEC filings (8-K). Orientation classification is rules-based and auditable per the note above. AIP figures are CEO annual cash incentive across two CEOs (Chapek FY21–22, Iger FY23–25), not fully continuous. Three LTIP cycles complete (66.9%, 73.4%, 48.9%), each earning out on ROIC after relative TSR paid 0%; FY24–25 cycles open. Data current through run date. Not investment advice.
takeaway: The defining tension: Disney's leadership has been paid solidly on operating results while the stock-based half of the plan repeatedly paid nothing — relative TSR earned 0% in all three completed long-term cycles, so the equity vested only on ROIC. That gap (good fundamentals, market underperformance) is the story, and it now shows up as a loud ~14% say-on-pay dissent at the March 2026 meeting. The plan itself is conservative and profitability-disciplined — segment operating income, free cash flow and ROIC dominate, with revenue a minor 17.5% and the FY25 grant tilting further toward EPS growth and away from relative TSR. The read: management is incentivized to compound profit and capital efficiency, and the board is quietly conceding the market-relative bar by cutting its weight. Watch the new CEO — Josh D'Amaro succeeded Iger in March 2026 — whose go-forward package will redefine the incentive against a still-skeptical tape.
